title: Made to Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die
author: Chip Heath, Dan Heath
thesisParagraph: Sticky ideas survive because they are built for attention, memory, belief, care, and action. The real discipline is not making a message louder or prettier. It is finding the core, making that core compact enough to travel, then giving it surprise, concrete hooks, credible proof, human stakes, and a story shape that lets people retell it without losing the point.

coreIdeas.name: Core before polish
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A message cannot stick until it has one governing point that can survive pressure and tradeoffs.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Cut a message until the priority that should guide decisions is unmistakable.

coreIdeas.name: Attention by broken pattern
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Surprise earns attention only when it opens a gap tied to the message instead of becoming a stunt.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Break the expected frame, then aim curiosity back at the core.

coreIdeas.name: Meaning with handles
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Concrete details make an idea visible enough for people to remember, compare, and coordinate around.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Replace floating abstraction with a shared scene, object, or testable image.

coreIdeas.name: Proof people can judge
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Credibility grows when evidence moves close enough to be checked, witnessed, or felt at human scale.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Turn assertion into proof the reader can inspect without trusting status alone.

coreIdeas.name: Care through human stakes
coreIdeas.oneSentence: People care when significance becomes personal through one person, identity, dignity, or meaningful consequence.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Move from abstract importance to a stake someone can feel without being manipulated.

coreIdeas.name: Story as carrier
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A story carries a lesson farther when the point is embedded in what happens, not pasted on afterward.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Build the lesson into sequence, choice, and consequence so it can survive retelling.

targetReader: People who need ideas to travel through teams, classrooms, customers, donors, voters, or families and who cannot rely on authority, repetition, or longer explanations to make the point land.

signatureMoves: uses SUCCESs traits, sticky examples, and playful reversals
makes the message concrete enough to be retold after the meeting
keeps the prose brisk, curious, and lightly comic about bad communication
turns abstraction into a test of memory, surprise, and usefulness
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not make stickiness sound like branding sparkle.
Do not praise simplicity unless the core idea survives retelling.

voiceSpecimens: The message survived because it could fit in a human mouth.
Clever is cheap; memorable has work to do.
voiceAntiSpecimens: This chapter explains how communicators can leverage multidimensional persuasion frameworks.
The author argues that ideas need to be sticky in order to influence stakeholders.
In conclusion, readers should try to communicate better every day.
The concept is important because communication is a fundamental leadership capability.
Use the SUCCESs framework to optimize message retention across audiences.
teachingArc: The book compounds from selection to transmission. First the reader learns to find the core, then to win attention without gimmickry, make the core visible, make it believable, make it matter, and finally package it in narrative so other people can carry it onward.
forbiddenMoves: Do not reduce the book to a checklist of six adjectives without showing the design choice each one forces.
Do not make sticky mean catchy, viral, clever, or emotionally manipulative.
Do not reuse one generic meeting, nonprofit, classroom, or pitch scene across chapters with new names.
Do not invent named studies or famous anecdotes beyond the source sidecars.
Do not let surprise, emotion, or story drift away from the core message they are supposed to serve.
Do not bury the message under communication theory.
Do not use a clever example unless it teaches a sticky trait.
